title: The Ramayana Film Wants ₹450 Crore Just for Hindi Distribution. Netflix Already Offered ₹700 Crore for Digital. They Said No.
excerpt: Nitesh Tiwari’s two-part epic is demanding the most expensive distribution deal in Indian cinema history — and the numbers suggest the producers think they’re building India’s answer to the MCU.
body:
Here is a number that should make you sit up: ₹450 crore.

That’s what producer Namit Malhotra is reportedly asking for the Hindi theatrical distribution rights alone — not the satellite rights, not the digital rights, not the overseas rights — just the right to put *Ramayana* in Hindi cinemas across India. If that deal closes, it will be the most expensive distribution agreement in the history of Indian cinema, surpassing Shah Rukh Khan’s *King* at ₹250 crore.

And that’s not even the headline number. Netflix reportedly offered ₹700 crore for the digital rights to both parts of the film. Malhotra said no.

## The Scale of the Bet

Let’s lay out what *Ramayana* actually is, because the ambition is staggering.

Directed by Nitesh Tiwari (*Dangal*, *Chhichhore*), the film is a two-part epic releasing Diwali 2026 (Part 1) and 2027 (Part 2). The combined budget is reportedly ₹1,600 crore — making it the most expensive Indian film franchise ever produced. For context, *RRR* cost ₹550 crore. *Baahubali 2* cost ₹250 crore.

The cast reads like a fantasy draft: Ranbir Kapoor as Ram, Sai Pallavi as Sita, Yash as Ravana. The VFX are by DNEG — Malhotra’s own company, the same outfit behind *Inception*, *Interstellar*, and *Oppenheimer*. The score is by Hans Zimmer.

Warner Bros. is in advanced talks for global theatrical distribution. IMAX has confirmed the film for its 2026 premium slate. This isn’t a Bollywood film with international ambitions. This is an Indian film built on a Hollywood production model, with Indian mythology as its intellectual property.

## Why Distributors Are Nervous

Not everyone thinks the numbers add up. According to *Variety India*, several major distributors — including Dharma Productions, AA Films, and Pen Studios — are in discussions, but some have privately expressed concern about the asking price.

The logic goes like this: for a distributor to recover ₹450 crore in Hindi theatrical rights, the film would need to earn somewhere north of ₹1,000 crore at the domestic box office just for the distributor to break even. That’s a threshold only three Hindi films have ever crossed: *Baahubali 2* (Hindi), *Pathaan*, and *Jawan*.

Malhotra’s team is projecting ₹1,000–1,500 crore domestic and ₹2,500 crore worldwide. Those aren’t unreasonable numbers for a Diwali release with this cast and this IP — but they require everything to go right.

## The Netflix Rejection Tells You Everything

The fact that Malhotra turned down ₹700 crore from Netflix for digital rights to both parts is the most revealing data point. It means the production team believes the theatrical window alone will generate enough revenue — and enough cultural impact — to justify keeping digital rights as a separate, later auction.

In an era when most Indian producers are racing to close OTT deals before the first shot is filmed, this is a radically different bet. It’s saying: this film is big enough to fill cinemas first, and the streaming platforms will pay more later because of what the theatrical run proves.

## What This Means for NRI Audiences

For the Indian diaspora, *Ramayana* is being built as a global event — not a Bollywood film that happens to get a few overseas screens. Warner Bros. distribution means proper marketing, proper screen counts, and proper opening-weekend availability in the US, UK, Canada, Australia, and the Middle East.

IMAX confirmation means you’ll be able to watch it on the same screens as *Dune* and *Avengers*. That’s not just distribution — it’s positioning.

For NRIs who grew up watching Ramanand Sagar’s *Ramayan* on Doordarshan — the series that literally stopped the country — this is the franchise play India has never attempted at this scale. It’s the closest Indian cinema has come to building its own MCU, with mythology as the shared universe.

## The Bottom Line

The distribution deal hasn’t closed yet. If it does at ₹450 crore, it rewrites the economics of Indian cinema. If it doesn’t, and Malhotra has to take a lower number, it still sets a new ceiling for what Indian films can demand.

Either way, when *Ramayana* arrives on Diwali 2026, it will be the most expensive, most hyped, and most consequential Indian film release in history. The only question is whether the audience shows up at a scale that justifies the audacity of the asking price.

The producers are betting ₹1,600 crore that they will.
nri_angle: With Warner Bros. in talks for global distribution and an IMAX release confirmed, Ramayana is being positioned as a worldwide event.
